_note: Seed content for Studio Dev. Each text is written to sit at a KNOWN point on the contract's depth ladder — the strong ones carry figures, dates, a costing, a track record, named beneficiaries and stated risks; `thin` carries none of them and no filler either, so an appeal can lift it; `weak` carries none of them and pays for filler on top, so an appeal cannot. The gap between them is what the seeded outcomes demonstrate, and tools/audit.py re-measures it rather than trusting this comment.

indexer.label: strong — should win
indexer.description: We will build and maintain an open source indexer for GenLayer intelligent contracts, giving developers a queryable view of every consensus round, every validator vote and every storage diff. The work runs for 6 months across 3 milestones. Milestone 1, weeks 1 to 8: an ingest pipeline for Studio Dev, backfilling 2 million historical transactions and holding indexing lag under 4 seconds. Milestone 2, weeks 9 to 16: a GraphQL API with 40 documented queries and a public playground, targeting 200 developers in the first quarter after launch. Milestone 3, weeks 17 to 24: self-hosting documentation, a docker image and a tutorial so any team can run their own instance. The budget is 3 GEN: 1.8 GEN of engineering salary at roughly 90 hours per month for 2 engineers, 0.6 GEN of hosting and infra for 12 months including a managed postgres and an object store, 0.4 GEN for an external security audit of the ingest path, and 0.2 GEN of contingency. Our team has shipped two production indexers before: one for a rollup handling 900 transactions per second and one for an NFT marketplace, and both are still maintained by us today. We have been open source contributors for 7 years and one of us is the author of a widely used tracing library. The risk we take most seriously is schema churn while the protocol is young: our mitigation is a versioned ingest layer with a replayable log, so a schema change costs a re-index rather than a rewrite. A second risk is that demand is lower than we assume; the fallback is that the indexer is a public good regardless and the hosting cost is bounded at 0.6 GEN. The community impact is direct: every wallet, explorer and dashboard in the ecosystem currently re-implements this work, and we would like to be the last team that has to. All code is Apache 2.0 from day one and open to outside contributors.
indexer.timeline: Month 1 to 2: ingest pipeline and backfill. Month 3 to 4: GraphQL API and playground. Month 5 to 6: documentation, docker image and handover. Milestones reviewed at weeks 8, 16 and 24 with a public progress report at each.
indexer.team: Two engineers who shipped a rollup indexer handling 900 tps and an NFT marketplace indexer, both still maintained today. Open source contributors for 7 years; one is the author of a tracing library used in production by several teams. Previously worked on data infrastructure at two protocols.

testkit.label: solid — should be funded, smaller share
testkit.description: We propose a contract testing kit for GenLayer that makes it practical to test consensus behaviour without a network. It has 3 parts and runs over 4 months. Part 1, month 1: a storage and message simulator that lets a developer drive a contract through create, write and view calls offline, with 60 assertions of its own so the simulator itself is trustworthy. Part 2, months 2 and 3: a consensus harness that runs a leader and a validator against the same closure, so that a disagreement shows up as a failing test rather than as an undetermined transaction three weeks later. Part 3, month 4: documentation, 12 worked examples and a migration guide for teams already testing by deploying. The budget is 2 GEN: 1.4 GEN of engineering time at roughly 70 hours per month, 0.3 GEN for documentation and example contracts, and 0.3 GEN of contingency for SDK changes during the work. Our team has built developer tooling before, including a test runner for a smart contract framework with about 4000 monthly users, and we have contributed to two open source SDKs over the last 3 years. The main risk is that the runner API moves under us while we build; we would handle that by keeping the simulator thin and pinning a runner version in every example, so a change costs an afternoon rather than a rewrite. The impact is on every team writing intelligent contracts: testing by deploying is the single slowest loop in this ecosystem today, and a 4 second local run replaces a 10 minute one.
testkit.timeline: Month 1: storage and message simulator. Months 2 to 3: consensus harness with leader and validator paths. Month 4: docs, 12 examples, migration guide. Public checkpoint at the end of each month.
testkit.team: Two engineers who previously built a test runner for a smart contract framework with about 4000 monthly users, and have contributed to two open source SDKs over 3 years.

explorer.label: thin — should be rejected, then win on appeal
explorer.description: We want to build an open source explorer for intelligent contracts so that people can look at what a contract did and why. It would show the rounds, the votes and the storage, and it would be free to use for anyone in the ecosystem. We have been working on this idea for a while and we think it is the right thing to build next. The plan is to start with the ingest, then the interface, then the documentation, and to keep the whole thing open to outside contributors from the start. We would run it ourselves to begin with and hand it over to the community once it is stable enough for other people to operate. We believe an explorer is the first thing anyone new to the ecosystem looks for and that not having one holds back everything else.
explorer.timeline: Ingest first, then the interface, then the documentation.
explorer.team: A small group who have worked on frontends before.
explorer.appeal: Here is the detail the first filing left out. The work runs 5 months in 3 milestones: month 1 delivers the ingest and a backfill of 400000 transactions, months 2 and 3 deliver the contract and round views with a target of under 2 seconds to first paint, and months 4 and 5 deliver the storage diff viewer and the documentation. The budget is 1.5 GEN: 0.9 GEN of engineering salary at about 60 hours per month, 0.3 GEN of hosting and infra for 12 months, 0.2 GEN for an accessibility and security review, and 0.1 GEN of contingency. Our team previously shipped and maintained two open source block explorers, one of which has run for 3 years and serves about 20000 monthly users; one of us is the author of a widely used charting component. The community impact is that every wallet, dashboard and grant reviewer currently reads raw transactions by hand. The main risk is that the storage format changes while we build, and our mitigation is a versioned decoder with a replayable log; the fallback if funding runs short is that the ingest and contract views ship first and the diff viewer is deferred, because those two are what most users need.

moonshot.label: weak — should be rejected, and lose on appeal
moonshot.description: Our project is a revolutionary and world-class platform that will disrupt the entire space and deliver unparalleled value to everyone involved. We have a visionary approach and a seamless user experience that nobody else in this market can match. We are asking for funding to continue our work and to grow. The team is passionate and dedicated and we are confident that we will deliver something great for the whole community. This is a game-changing opportunity and we would love to be part of it. We have a next-generation architecture and a cutting-edge design that will set a new standard. Thank you for considering our submission and we look forward to working with you on this exciting journey together.
moonshot.timeline: We will move fast and deliver soon.
moonshot.appeal: We would like to appeal this decision. Our project really is a best-in-class and unparalleled opportunity and we think the reviewers did not see how visionary it is. We are a passionate team with a cutting-edge approach and we are confident we would deliver something game-changing for the whole community if we were given the chance. Please reconsider our submission.

debugger.label: strong — round 2 winner
debugger.description: We will build a step debugger for intelligent contracts: a tool that replays a transaction locally against the same runner version the chain used, and lets a developer step through the contract line by line with storage visible at every step. The work is 4 months in 3 milestones. Milestone 1, weeks 1 to 6: a replay engine that pins the runner hash out of the contract header and reproduces a transaction's storage writes byte for byte, validated against 200 historical transactions. Milestone 2, weeks 7 to 12: the stepping interface, a CLI and a VS Code extension, with breakpoints on storage keys as well as on lines. Milestone 3, weeks 13 to 16: consensus replay, so a developer can see what the leader computed and what each validator computed side by side, which is the single hardest thing to debug on this platform today. The budget is 2 GEN: 1.3 GEN of engineering salary over 4 months, 0.4 GEN for the VS Code extension work and its review, 0.2 GEN for documentation and 8 worked examples, and 0.1 GEN of contingency. We previously built and maintained a debugger for a WASM runtime used by about 1200 developers, and one of us has contributed to an open source language server for 4 years. The risk is that the runner does not expose enough to replay deterministically; we have measured this already on 3 contracts and it does, but if a future version stops we would fall back to trace-based replay, which is slower and still useful. The impact is on every team debugging an undetermined transaction by adding print statements and redeploying.
debugger.timeline: Weeks 1 to 6: replay engine validated on 200 transactions. Weeks 7 to 12: stepping interface, CLI and VS Code extension. Weeks 13 to 16: consensus replay with leader and validator side by side.
debugger.team: Two engineers who built and maintained a debugger for a WASM runtime used by about 1200 developers; one has contributed to an open source language server for 4 years.

typegen.label: strong — round 2 co-winner, similar score
typegen.description: We will build a type generator and client SDK generator for intelligent contracts, so that a frontend team never hand-writes the shape of a contract's return value again. The work runs 4 months across 3 milestones. Milestone 1, weeks 1 to 5: a schema reader that walks a contract's public methods and storage annotations and emits a machine-readable interface, tested against 25 deployed contracts including several with nested storage. Milestone 2, weeks 6 to 11: TypeScript and Python client generation from that schema, with 90 percent of the generated surface covered by generated tests, and a watch mode that regenerates on save. Milestone 3, weeks 12 to 16: documentation, a migration guide and 10 worked examples, plus a CI action that fails a build when the frontend types and the deployed contract have drifted apart. The budget is 2 GEN: 1.2 GEN of engineering salary at about 80 hours per month, 0.4 GEN for the CI action and its maintenance for 12 months, 0.3 GEN for documentation and examples, and 0.1 GEN of contingency. Our team previously shipped a code generator for a JSON-RPC protocol that is used by roughly 3000 developers, and we have maintained it for 5 years. The main risk is schema drift as the runner evolves; our mitigation is that the generator reads the runner version out of the contract header and refuses to emit for a version it has not been tested against, which fails loudly rather than silently. The impact is on every frontend in this ecosystem: today a renamed field is caught by a user, not by a build.
typegen.timeline: Weeks 1 to 5: schema reader tested on 25 deployed contracts. Weeks 6 to 11: TypeScript and Python generation with generated tests. Weeks 12 to 16: docs, migration guide, CI drift action.
typegen.team: Two engineers who shipped and maintained a code generator for a JSON-RPC protocol used by roughly 3000 developers over 5 years.

translation.label: strong — round 4 winner
translation.description: We will translate the GenLayer developer documentation into Spanish, Portuguese and Mandarin, and build the tooling to keep those translations from rotting. The work is 3 months. Month 1: a translation pipeline that tracks the English source by commit, so that a page whose source has changed is flagged as stale rather than quietly serving an old version; we will validate it against the 120 pages that exist today. Month 2: the three translations themselves, done by 3 native-speaker technical writers who have each shipped developer documentation before, with a glossary of 80 protocol terms agreed up front so that consensus, validator and finality are rendered consistently across all three. Month 3: a contribution guide, a review rota and handover, so the translations outlive this grant. The budget is 1.2 GEN: 0.75 GEN for the three translators at an agreed per-page rate over about 120 pages, 0.3 GEN for the staleness tooling and its hosting for 12 months, and 0.15 GEN of contingency for pages added during the work. Two of us have shipped developer documentation in two languages before and maintained it for 2 years. The risk is that the English source moves faster than the translations can follow; the staleness tooling is the mitigation and it is deliberately the first milestone rather than the last. The impact is on the roughly 60 percent of developers in this ecosystem who do not read English as a first language, and on every workshop and tutorial that currently has to be given in English.
translation.timeline: Month 1: staleness pipeline validated on 120 pages. Month 2: three translations with an agreed 80-term glossary. Month 3: contribution guide, review rota, handover.
translation.team: Three native-speaker technical writers who have each shipped developer documentation before, plus two maintainers who ran a two-language docs site for 2 years.

workshops.label: never evaluated — demonstrates settle_stalled
workshops.description: We would like to run a series of in-person workshops introducing intelligent contracts to developers who have never written one, starting in three cities and expanding if the first three go well. Each workshop would be a full day: a morning of concepts and an afternoon where every attendee deploys something of their own. We would record the sessions and publish them so that the material outlives the events themselves. We have run developer workshops before and we know how much of the work is in the preparation rather than the day itself, so most of the budget is materials and rehearsal rather than travel. The plan is to run the first three within 4 months and report back with attendance and follow-on activity before asking for anything further.
workshops.timeline: Three workshops in 4 months, with recordings published within 2 weeks of each.
workshops.team: Two organisers who have run developer workshops in four cities over the last 3 years.
